etymology: Hebrew Sela Rimmon, “the rock of the pomegranate”; a cliff or crag in the wilderness of Benjamin where the remnant of the tribe took refuge; distinct from Rimmon the town.
biblical_def: The rock Rimmon was a great crag in the wilderness near Gibeah, the last refuge of the tribe of Benjamin after the terrible civil war provoked by the outrage at Gibeah: “But six hundred men turned and fled to the wilderness unto the rock Rimmon, and abode in the rock Rimmon four months” (Judg 20:47). Benjamin had been all but destroyed — its cities burned, its men slain — and only six hundred survived, hiding in the rock until Israel took counsel to preserve the tribe from extinction and made peace. This is a place, not the town of Rimmon nor the Syrian god of that name. The rock Rimmon preaches both the severity and the mercy of God. Benjamin’s near-annihilation was the fruit of sin defended rather than judged; the men of Gibeah did wickedness, and the tribe shielded them, and the sword devoured. Yet God did not suffer the tribe to perish utterly; a remnant was saved in the rock, and from that remnant came King Saul, and Mordecai, and the apostle Paul. The rock of refuge in the wilderness figures the greater Rock in whom the guilty remnant hides from the avenging sword, and is spared to bring forth fruit to God.

etymology: Hebrew Gidom, perhaps “a cutting off” or “desolation”; a place in Benjamin, the limit of Israel’s pursuit of the fleeing Benjamites, named once.
biblical_def: Gidom was a place in the territory of Benjamin, marking how far Israel pursued the shattered tribe in the civil war: “And they turned and fled toward the wilderness unto the rock of Rimmon: and they gleaned of them in the highways five thousand men; and pursued hard after them unto Gidom, and slew two thousand men of them” (Judg 20:45). Its name may mean “a cutting off,” grimly fitting for the place where the slaughter of Benjamin reached its farthest point. The scene is one of the darkest in the book of Judges, when there was no king in Israel and every man did that which was right in his own eyes, and the nation nearly cut off one of its own tribes. Gidom preaches the horror of sin unrestrained and the ruin that comes when a people abandons the fear of God. Yet it also stands as a boundary: the pursuit reached Gidom and no farther; the slaughter, terrible as it was, was not without limit, and the remnant escaped to the rock. Even in judgment God sets a bound to the destroyer. The believer, reading this dreadful chapter, learns to tremble at sin, to prize godly order and rule, and to bless the God who does not let wrath consume His people utterly.

etymology: Hebrew Chelqath ha-Tsurim, “the field of strong men” (or “field of sword-edges”); a field at Gibeon where twelve champions of each side slew one another.
biblical_def: Helkath-hazzurim, “the field of strong men,” was a plot of ground at Gibeon where a grim contest opened the war between the house of Saul and the house of David. Twelve chosen men of Benjamin and twelve of David’s servants met, and each laid hold of his opponent and drove his sword into his side, so that all four-and-twenty fell together: “And they caught every one his fellow by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fell down together: wherefore that place was called Helkathhazzurim, which is in Gibeon” (2Sa 2:16). The mutual slaughter settled nothing; it only kindled a long and bloody war between brethren. The field of strong men preaches the folly and misery of civil strife, when the strength given for defence is turned against one’s own countrymen and kinsmen. Strength is a gift of God, but strength employed in pride and rivalry devours those who wield it, and the strong men fall together. The people of God are warned against biting and devouring one another, lest they be consumed one of another; the sad field at Gibeon stands as a monument to the death that comes when brother turns his sword on brother.

etymology: The rough, uncultivated country about Gibeon, north-west of Jerusalem; the way by which Joab pursued Abner after the battle by the pool of Gibeon.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Gibeon was the wild country about the city of Gibeon, along which Joab and Abishai pursued Abner after the deadly encounter at the pool: “Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner: and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon” (2Sa 2:24). Gibeon was a place of many memories: here the sun stood still at Joshua’s word, here the great high place stood before the temple was built, and here Solomon received wisdom from the LORD in a dream. But this scene is a sorrowful one, the pursuit of the war between the houses of Saul and David, ending in the death of Asahel by Abner’s spear and the long feud that followed. The wilderness of Gibeon preaches the sorrow of division prolonged. The war was “long,” and it wasted the strength of Israel, until at last David was established over all. Yet through the whole sad story God was working His purpose, bringing the promised king to the throne. The believer learns that the LORD accomplishes His unshakeable design even through the strife and confusion of men, and that the kingdom appointed of God will surely come, though the way to it run through the wilderness.

etymology: Hebrew Perets Uzzah, “the breach of Uzzah”; the threshing-floor place, between Kirjath-jearim and Jerusalem, where Uzzah was struck dead for touching the ark.
biblical_def: Perez-uzzah, “the breach of Uzzah,” was the place where a solemn judgment fell as David brought up the ark of God on a new cart. When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah put forth his hand to steady the ark, and “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God” (2Sa 6:7). David was grieved and afraid, “and he called the name of the place Perezuzzah to this day” (2Sa 6:8). The lesson is sharp and abiding: the ark was to be carried by the Levites on staves upon their shoulders, according to the express command, not hauled on a cart after the manner of the Philistines. Good intentions do not sanctify disobedience; the worship of God must be offered in the way God appoints, not in the way that seems best to men. This is the regulative principle written in blood: what God has not commanded in His worship, He has not permitted. Uzzah’s error was to touch the holy thing with unhallowed presumption, treating the ark as a common load. Perez-uzzah stands for ever as a warning that God is holy, that He will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him, and that reverence, not innovation, is the rule of acceptable worship.

etymology: Hebrew Botsets, perhaps “shining” or “slippery”; one of two sharp rocks at the pass of Michmash, by which Jonathan climbed to attack the Philistine garrison.
biblical_def: Bozez was one of two sharp crags guarding the pass of Michmash, named with its fellow Seneh: “And between the passages, by which Jonathan sought to go over unto the Philistines’ garrison, there was a sharp rock on the one side, and a sharp rock on the other side: and the name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh” (1Sa 14:4). By this steep and perilous place Jonathan, with only his armour-bearer, climbed up on hands and feet to fall upon the enemy, saying words that ring with faith: “it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6). And the LORD wrought a great deliverance that day by two men against a host. The rock Bozez preaches the boldness of faith that counts on God. Jonathan did not measure the odds by the number of swords but by the power of the LORD, for whom no odds are long. The hard and dangerous climb between the crags is the very picture of the venture of faith, which goes forward at God’s call into what seems impossible, trusting that He can save by many or by few. Bozez stands as a memorial that faith’s daring is honoured by the God who is never restrained.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Kar, “house of the lamb” or “place of pasture”; the point to which Israel pursued the Philistines after the victory at Mizpeh in the days of Samuel.
biblical_def: Beth-car was the place to which Israel drove the fleeing Philistines after the great deliverance at Mizpeh in the days of Samuel: “And the men of Israel went out of Mizpeh, and pursued the Philistines, and smote them, until they came under Bethcar” (1Sa 7:11). The victory was wholly the LORD’s: while Samuel offered up the burnt offering and cried to God for Israel, “the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them; and they were smitten before Israel” (1Sa 7:10). Then Samuel set up a stone and called it Ebenezer, the stone of help, saying, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.” Beth-car, whose name may mean “house of the lamb,” marks the far point of a salvation won by sacrifice and prayer, not by the sword of Israel. It preaches that God answers the cries of His people when they put away their idols and turn to Him with all their heart, as Israel had done at Samuel’s word. The thunder of the LORD, not the strength of men, routed the enemy; and the memorial stone stood to teach every generation to look back on past mercy and forward in hope, confessing at each new trial, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us, and He will help us still.

etymology: Hebrew Yeshanah, “old” or “ancient”; a town on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin, taken by Abijah of Judah from Jeroboam.
biblical_def: Jeshanah, whose name means “old” or “ancient,” was a town taken by Abijah king of Judah from Jeroboam king of Israel after the great battle in mount Ephraim: “And Abijah pursued after Jeroboam, and took cities from him, Bethel with the towns thereof, and Jeshanah with the towns thereof, and Ephrain with the towns thereof” (2Ch 13:19). The victory came not by Judah’s numbers, for Jeroboam had twice as many, but by their reliance on the LORD: “the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 13:18). Abijah had cried to the northern host that God Himself was with Judah for their captain, that Judah kept the appointed priesthood and worship while Jeroboam had made his golden calves and cast out the priests of the LORD. Jeshanah, the “old” town, preaches the strength of the old paths. Judah prevailed by cleaving to the ancient worship and the covenant of the fathers, while Jeroboam’s novelties brought defeat. The Lord bids His people ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and find rest for their souls. The ancient town won by the God of the fathers is a token that faithfulness to the old truth, not innovation, is the way of victory and rest.

etymology: Hebrew Ephes Dammim, “boundary of blood” (also called Pas-dammim); the place between Shochoh and Azekah where the Philistines encamped before David slew Goliath.
biblical_def: Ephes-dammim, “the boundary of blood,” also called Pas-dammim, was the place where the Philistine host encamped facing Israel before the combat of David and Goliath: “Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim” (1Sa 17:1). It was later remembered as a field where the LORD wrought a great victory, when the Philistines gathered there and the people fled, but a mighty man of David stood his ground in a plot of barley (1Ch 11:13). The name, “boundary of blood,” suits a frontier long contested between Israel and the Philistines, wet with the blood of many battles. Here the boy David came with his sling and five smooth stones, and in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel whom Goliath had defied, felled the giant and delivered his people. Ephes-dammim preaches that the battle is the LORD’s. David’s confidence was not in sword or spear but in the living God, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel. The bloody boundary became the stage of that great sign, and points onward to the true David who, single-handed, overthrew the great enemy and won the field for His people.

etymology: Hebrew Gob, “pit” or “cistern”; a place where David’s men fought the Philistines and slew their giants.
biblical_def: Gob was a place, likely near Gezer, where David’s mighty men fought two battles against the Philistines and struck down their giants: “And it came to pass after this, that there was again a battle with the Philistines at Gob: then Sibbechai the Hushathite slew Saph, which was of the sons of the giant” (2Sa 21:18); “And there was again a battle in Gob with the Philistines, where Elhanan the son of Jaareoregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite” (2Sa 21:19). These were the sons of Rapha, the last of the giants, whom David and his men cut down one by one until the seed of the giants was destroyed out of the land. Gob, whose name means “pit,” preaches the continuing warfare of the people of God against the powers that once terrified them. Goliath had fallen by David’s hand years before, but his kindred remained, and the war was not over in a single day. So the church’s enemies, though the head be crushed at the cross, still rise up in their offspring, and the giants must be met and overthrown in every generation. But the mighty men of David prevailed, for the victory of their king was theirs; and the saints, following the true David who spoiled the powers of darkness, tread down the last of the giants in His strength until the seed of the enemy is destroyed out of the land.
